subject: psychology
title: Forensic Psychology: Offender Profiling
welcome_lead: Top-down sketches vs bottom-up data — two transatlantic profiling styles.
meta_desc: A-Level Psychology forensic offender profiling: top-down FBI vs bottom-up Canter.
final_note: Profiling is hypothesis generation, not a magic mirror.

concepts.def: Inferring offender characteristics from crime scene evidence.
US FBI approach — match scene to organised/disorganised types.
Planned, controlled crime, intelligent and socially competent.
Impulsive, chaotic crime, low IQ, socially isolated.
UK Canter approach — derive characteristics from statistical patterns.
Mapping crime locations to infer offender's base.

walkthroughs.body_html: The FBI Behavioral Science Unit interviewed 36 serial killers in the 1970s to build the organised/disorganised typology. Profilers classify the crime scene then predict offender attributes. Canter et al. (2004) analysed 100 US murders and found the two types overlap heavily — the typology is shaky.

Canter's approach uses statistical analysis of crime data to identify patterns. Investigative psychology applies smallest space analysis. Geographical profiling uses the circle theory (Canter & Larkin 1993) — most offenders are 'marauders' operating from a base, others are 'commuters'.

Canter's profile of John Duffy (1980s railway rapist) matched 13 of 17 offender attributes. But Copson (1995) surveyed 184 UK detectives: only 14% said profiling had ever helped them catch an offender. Profiling is best treated as an investigative aid, not proof.
